google calendar. easy and online so you'll be able to have the same info on ur computer as ur phone

Outlook is cross platform. It can do all these things, but I'm guessing it's not what you're looking for.

I could recommend you a few because I've tried my share of them but instead I'll tell you what I've learned after years using them: having all your organization in a rigid schedule (like in software) has way too much overhead - the more you depend on it more time it will consume for checking everything, making alterations, exceptions, etc.

What I do now is: if I absolutely need some form of schedule I'll use a free-form medium to lay it out (like a Word document or piece of paper) and use it for reference until I know everything by heart or as a simple check list. Things that are time-related like meetings or pay-dates I will put in a calendar software so I can get notifications and the like but I keep it to an absolute minimum and like to set recurrences only when something happens once every month, never less than that.

I'll break down my understanding and you can correct where I'm wrong:

  1. The bits in your fingerprint is the total amount of identifiable information your browser sends to the server. This can be information such as OS, user agent, flash or java version, what cookies the server has been sent etc.

  2. The uniqueness score is, well, just that. If you're too unique, you can be damned well sure that if one sees that browser fingerprint again, it's the same user. While some tools which protect your privacy, they may make you more unique, hence defeating some of the privacy measures. You want to strike a balance between blending into the swaths of other users so as not to attract attention and while withholding as much personally identifiable information as practical. Sort of in the same sense that TOR works. If only 10 people used it, it would be trivial to tell which user was which. If I understand correctly, that is why DARPA opened it to the public.
